title: Units, Time and Data Displays
bigQuestion: How do units, clocks and graphs help us measure change and show it to other people?

story.title: Pepper on the Scale
story.kicker: Every Monday the class weighs their guinea pig, and by spring a row of X marks tells a story nobody expected.
paragraphs: Room 12 adopted a guinea pig in January and named her Pepper. The vet said a healthy adult guinea pig weighs about 2 pounds. Pepper was young and small. Ms. Chen made a rule: every Monday, one student would set Pepper on the kitchen scale and read her weight to the nearest quarter pound. Then that student would draw an X above the weight on a line plot taped to the wall.

The first Monday, Pepper weighed 1 1/2 pounds. Dario put an X above 1 1/2. The next week she weighed 1 3/4. The week after, 1 3/4 again, so the second X stacked on top of the first. By the fourth week, Pepper had reached 2 pounds. The class cheered as the X marks marched to the right along the number line.

In March something strange happened. The scale read 2 1/4 pounds three Mondays in a row, and then 2 1/2. Aaliyah looked at the line plot and frowned. There were now more X marks above 2 1/4 than above any other number. She asked whether that meant Pepper was staying the same or still growing. The class argued about it for the whole math block.

Ms. Chen turned the argument into a lesson. A line plot shows how many times each measurement happened, not the order it happened in. To see growth over time, the class needed a different display. They also needed to convert: the vet used ounces, the food bag used grams, and the feeding chart used minutes and hours. Measurement, they learned, is only useful when everyone speaks the same units.
story.think: What can a line plot tell you about Pepper's weight, and what can it not tell you?

lessons.title: Inches, Feet and Yards
lessons.mainIdea: To change a bigger unit into a smaller one, multiply; 1 foot is 12 inches and 1 yard is 3 feet.
reading: Pepper's cage is 4 feet long. The pet store lists cages in inches. To *convert* feet to inches, remember that 1 foot is 12 inches. So 4 feet is 4 groups of 12 inches. That is 4 × 12 = 48 inches. Going from a big unit to a small unit gives more of them. So you multiply.

The same idea works for yards. A *yard* is 3 feet, which is 36 inches. A hallway that is 2 yards long is 2 × 3 = 6 feet, or 2 × 36 = 72 inches. A *mile* is 5,280 feet. That is why Chicago blocks are measured in feet and long trips in miles.

Going the other way, from small units to big units, means dividing. A jump rope is 84 inches long. How many feet is that? Since 12 inches make 1 foot, ask how many 12s are in 84. 84 ÷ 12 = 7. The rope is 7 feet. A common mistake is to multiply when you should divide. Ask: should I get more units or fewer?

words.d: to change a measurement from one unit to another without changing the amount
a length equal to 3 feet or 36 inches, about one big step
a long distance equal to 5,280 feet, about a 20-minute walk

look.title: Feet to Inches
look.prompt: What pattern do you see going down the table? How many inches would 7 feet be?

check.q: How many inches are in 5 feet?
check.why: 5 × 12 = 60 inches. Adding 5 + 12 = 17 is a common slip.

check.q: How many inches are in 2 yards?
check.why: 1 yard is 36 inches, so 2 × 36 = 72. 6 is the number of feet.

check.q: A board is 36 inches long. How many feet is that?
check.why: 36 ÷ 12 = 3 feet, because 3 × 12 = 36.

lessons.title: Meters, Grams and Kilograms
lessons.mainIdea: Metric units change by 100 or 1,000: 1 meter is 100 centimeters, 1 kilometer is 1,000 meters, 1 kilogram is 1,000 grams.
reading: The bag of guinea pig food says 2 kilograms. The feeding chart says 40 grams per day. To compare them, convert. A *kilogram* is 1,000 *grams*. So 2 kilograms is 2 × 1,000 = 2,000 grams. Kilo means one thousand. That prefix works for length, too: a *kilometer* is 1,000 meters.

Metric length uses centimeters and meters. A *meter* is 100 centimeters, about the height of a kitchen counter. A ruler that is 3 meters long is 3 × 100 = 300 centimeters. Pepper is 25 centimeters long. Four Peppers in a line would be 100 centimeters, or exactly 1 meter.

Mixed amounts convert piece by piece. A backpack weighs 2 kilograms 300 grams. Convert the kilograms first: 2 × 1,000 = 2,000 grams. Then add the leftover grams: 2,000 + 300 = 2,300 grams. Going backward, 5,000 meters is 5,000 ÷ 1,000 = 5 kilometers. Metric conversions are all tens, so you never need messy numbers like 12 or 36.

words.d: a small metric unit of mass; a paper clip weighs about 1 gram
a metric unit of mass equal to 1,000 grams; a liter of water weighs about 1 kilogram
a metric unit of length equal to 100 centimeters
a metric unit of length equal to 1,000 meters, used for long distances

look.title: Food for the Month
look.text: Pepper eats 40 grams of pellets each day. In 10 days she eats 10 × 40 = 400 grams. In 30 days she eats 30 × 40 = 1,200 grams. The food bag holds 2 kilograms, which is 2,000 grams. After 30 days, 2,000 − 1,200 = 800 grams are left.
look.prompt: How many more days of food are in the bag after the first 30 days? Show your division.

check.q: How many centimeters are in 4 meters?
check.why: 1 meter is 100 centimeters, so 4 × 100 = 400 cm.

check.q: A bag weighs 2 kilograms 300 grams. How many grams is that in all?
check.why: 2 × 1,000 = 2,000 grams, plus 300 more is 2,300 grams.

check.q: A race is 5,000 meters long. How many kilometers is that?
check.why: 5,000 ÷ 1,000 = 5 kilometers, since each kilometer is 1,000 meters.

lessons.title: Cups, Quarts and Liters
lessons.mainIdea: Liquid volume has its own units: 1 gallon is 4 quarts, 1 quart is 2 pints, 1 pint is 2 cups, and 1 liter is 1,000 milliliters.
reading: Pepper's water bottle holds 250 *milliliters*. The class fills it from a 1-liter pitcher. A *liter* is 1,000 milliliters. So the pitcher fills the bottle 1,000 ÷ 250 = 4 times. A 2-liter soda bottle holds 2 × 1,000 = 2,000 milliliters. Liquid volume measures how much a container holds.

U.S. kitchens use cups, pints, quarts and gallons. Each step doubles or quadruples. A *pint* is 2 cups. A *quart* is 2 pints, which is 4 cups. A *gallon* is 4 quarts. So a gallon is 4 × 4 = 16 cups. A milk jug from the store holds 1 gallon, and a school milk carton holds 1 cup.

To convert, find the chain. How many pints are in 3 gallons? First gallons to quarts: 3 × 4 = 12 quarts. Then quarts to pints: 12 × 2 = 24 pints. A common mistake is skipping a step, like saying 3 gallons is 6 pints. Write each step down so you do not lose one.

words.d: a tiny amount of liquid; about 20 drops of water make 1 milliliter
a metric unit of liquid volume equal to 1,000 milliliters
2 cups of liquid
4 quarts, 8 pints or 16 cups; the size of a big milk jug

look.title: Cups in Each Container
look.prompt: Each row doubles the one before it. How many cups are in 2 gallons? In 3 quarts?

check.q: How many milliliters are in 2 liters?
check.why: 1 liter is 1,000 milliliters, so 2 × 1,000 = 2,000 mL.

check.q: How many cups are in 1 gallon?
check.why: A gallon is 4 quarts, and each quart is 4 cups, so 4 × 4 = 16 cups.

check.q: How many pints are in 6 quarts?
check.why: Each quart is 2 pints, so 6 × 2 = 12 pints. Dividing gives 3, which is backward.

lessons.title: Minutes, Hours and Days
lessons.mainIdea: Time converts like other units: 1 hour is 60 minutes, 1 day is 24 hours, 1 week is 7 days.
reading: Time is a measurement, too, but its units are not tens. An *hour* is 60 *minutes*. A day is 24 hours. A week is 7 days. To change hours into minutes, multiply by 60. Pepper's play time is 3 hours a week. That is 3 × 60 = 180 minutes of running around the classroom.

Going from minutes to hours means dividing by 60, and there is often a remainder. A movie is 150 minutes long. 150 ÷ 60 is 2 with 30 left over, because 2 × 60 = 120 and 150 − 120 = 30. So the movie is 2 hours 30 minutes. Do not write 2 hours 50 minutes; the leftover is 30.

Days and hours work the same way. Two days is 2 × 24 = 48 hours. A week is 7 × 24 = 168 hours. A common mistake is to treat time like money and think 1 hour 30 minutes is 1.3 hours. It is actually 1 and a half hours, because 30 is half of 60.

words.d: a unit of time equal to 60 minutes; a day has 24 of them
a unit of time equal to 60 seconds; 60 minutes make an hour
what is left over after dividing, like the 30 in 150 ÷ 60 = 2 remainder 30

look.title: Hours to Minutes
look.prompt: Use the table to find how many minutes are in 2 and a half hours. Which two rows did you add?

check.q: How many minutes are in 4 hours?
check.why: 4 × 60 = 240 minutes. Adding 4 + 60 = 64 is wrong.

check.q: A game lasts 90 minutes. How long is that in hours and minutes?
check.why: 90 − 60 = 30, so 90 minutes is 1 hour 30 minutes.

check.q: How many hours are in 2 days?
check.why: Each day is 24 hours, so 2 × 24 = 48 hours.

lessons.title: How Much Time Passed
lessons.mainIdea: To find elapsed time, jump from the start time to the next easy mark, then count the hours and minutes to the end.
reading: Math class starts at 9:45 and ends at 11:20. How long is it? That length of time is *elapsed time*. Do not subtract 9:45 from 11:20 like ordinary numbers, because 60 minutes make an hour, not 100. Instead, jump along a *number line* of time.

Start at 9:45. Jump 15 minutes to reach 10:00, a nice round time. Jump 1 hour to reach 11:00. Jump 20 minutes to reach 11:20. Now add the jumps: 15 minutes + 1 hour + 20 minutes. That is 1 hour and 35 minutes. Class is 1 hour 35 minutes long.

Elapsed time also works forward and backward. Pepper's cage cleaning starts at 10:50 and takes 35 minutes. Jump 10 minutes to 11:00, then 25 more to 11:25. It ends at 11:25. If a movie ends at 4:10 and lasted 1 hour 45 minutes, jump back 1 hour to 3:10, then back 45 minutes: 10 minutes to 3:00, then 35 more to 2:25. It started at 2:25.

words.d: the amount of time that passes between a start time and an end time
a line with marks in order; for time, the marks are clock times like 9:00, 9:15, 9:30

look.title: Jumps on the Time Line
look.text: A field trip bus leaves at 8:35 and arrives at 10:05. Jump 25 minutes to 9:00. Jump 1 hour to 10:00. Jump 5 minutes to 10:05. Add the jumps: 25 + 5 = 30 minutes, plus 1 hour. The ride took 1 hour 30 minutes. Now try a lunch that starts at 11:40 and ends at 12:25.
look.prompt: How long is lunch? Which round time did you jump to first?

check.q: Practice starts at 2:15 and ends at 3:40. How long is practice?
check.why: Jump 45 minutes to 3:00, then 40 minutes to 3:40. That is 85 minutes, or 1 hour 25 minutes.

check.q: Cage cleaning starts at 10:50 and takes 35 minutes. When does it end?
check.why: 10 minutes reach 11:00, and 25 more reach 11:25. Clocks never show 10:85.

check.q: A movie ends at 4:10 and lasted 1 hour 45 minutes. When did it start?
check.why: Back 1 hour is 3:10. Back 10 minutes is 3:00. Back 35 more is 2:25.

lessons.title: Bar Graphs With a Scale
lessons.mainIdea: On a bar graph, read the scale first, because each line may stand for more than 1.
reading: Room 12 voted on a name for their second guinea pig. Ms. Chen showed the votes on a *bar graph*. Each name got a bar. The taller the bar, the more votes. But the numbers on the side went 0, 5, 10, 15, 20. That list of numbers is the *scale*. Each line up meant 5 votes, not 1.

The bar for Biscuit reached the third line. That is 3 × 5 = 15 votes. The bar for Nugget reached the second line, so 2 × 5 = 10 votes. The bar for Oreo stopped halfway between the first and second lines, so it was between 5 and 10, which is 7 or 8. Ms. Chen said 8.

Use the graph to compare. Biscuit beat Nugget by 15 − 10 = 5 votes. All three names together got 15 + 10 + 8 = 33 votes. A common mistake is to count lines instead of reading the scale, saying Biscuit got 3 votes. Always look at the numbers on the side before you read a bar.

words.d: a display where the height of each bar shows how many, with a bar for each group
the numbers along the side of a graph that tell what each line stands for

look.title: Votes for the New Guinea Pig's Name
look.cite: Example class vote, counted by hand
look.prompt: If you drew this as a bar graph with a scale of 2, how many lines tall would the Biscuit bar be? What about Waffles?

check.q: A bar graph has a scale of 4. A bar reaches the third line. How many does it show?
check.why: Each line stands for 4, so 3 × 4 = 12.

check.q: Biscuit got 15 votes and Nugget got 10. How many more votes did Biscuit get?
check.why: 15 − 10 = 5 more votes. Adding gives 25, the total.

check.q: Why does a bar graph need a scale?
choices: To show which bar came first
To list the names of the groups
To tell how many each line stands for
check.why: Without the scale, you cannot know if a line means 1, 5 or 100.

lessons.title: Picture Graphs and Keys
lessons.mainIdea: In a picture graph, the key tells how many each picture stands for, and half a picture stands for half that amount.
reading: A *picture graph* uses little pictures instead of bars. The class made one for library books read in March. Each row is a student. Each book picture stands for 4 books. That rule is called the *key*, and it is printed under the graph. Reading a picture graph without the key is like reading a bar graph without the scale.

Maya's row shows 3 whole book pictures. That is 3 × 4 = 12 books. Leo's row shows 2 whole books and a half book. The half picture stands for half of 4, which is 2. So Leo read 2 × 4 + 2 = 10 books. Dario's row shows 5 pictures, so 5 × 4 = 20 books.

Picture graphs answer questions quickly. Who read the most? Dario, with the longest row. How many more than Maya? 20 − 12 = 8. How many in all? 12 + 10 + 20 = 42. A common mistake is counting each picture as 1 book. Then Maya would seem to have read only 3, which the key says is wrong.

words.d: a display that uses rows of small pictures to show how many
the note on a picture graph that says how many each picture stands for

look.title: Read the Key First
look.text: A picture graph shows pets owned by students in three classes. Each paw print stands for 2 pets. Room 10 shows 6 paw prints. Room 11 shows 4 and a half paw prints. Room 12 shows 5 paw prints. Room 10 has 6 × 2 = 12 pets. Room 11 has 4 × 2 + 1 = 9 pets. Room 12 has 5 × 2 = 10 pets.
look.prompt: If the key changed to 3 pets per paw print, how many pets would Room 10 have? What would a half paw print mean then?

check.q: In a picture graph, each star stands for 3 goals. A row shows 5 stars. How many goals?
check.why: 5 × 3 = 15 goals. Counting stars as 1 each gives 5.

check.q: Each book picture stands for 4 books. A row shows 2 books and a half book. How many books?
check.why: 2 × 4 = 8, and half a picture is 2 more, so 8 + 2 = 10.

check.q: Which part of a picture graph tells how many each picture stands for?
check.why: The key is the rule, like each picture stands for 4 books.

lessons.title: Line Plots With Fractions
lessons.mainIdea: A line plot stacks an X above each measurement on a number line, so tall stacks show the most common values.
reading: Pepper's weight chart is a *line plot*. The bottom is a number line marked in quarters: 1 1/2, 1 3/4, 2, 2 1/4, 2 1/2. Each Monday's weight becomes one X above its number. When the same weight happens again, the new X stacks on top. So a tall stack means that weight happened many times.

Read Pepper's plot. There is 1 X above 1 1/2, 2 above 1 3/4, 2 above 2, 3 above 2 1/4 and 1 above 2 1/2. Count all the X marks: 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 + 1 = 9. The class weighed Pepper 9 times. The most common weight is 2 1/4, because that stack is tallest.

Line plots also show *range*, the distance from smallest to largest. Pepper's smallest weight is 1 1/2 and largest is 2 1/2. The range is 2 1/2 − 1 1/2 = 1 pound. A common mistake is to think the tallest stack is the biggest measurement. It is only the most frequent one. The biggest is the X farthest right.

words.d: a number line with an X stacked above each measurement, one X per time it happened
the difference between the largest and smallest values in a set of data
the value that shows up the most times; on a line plot it has the tallest stack

look.title: Pepper's Weight, Nine Mondays
look.cite: Example class data, weighed to the nearest quarter pound
look.prompt: Draw this as a line plot. How many X marks are at 2 pounds or heavier? What is the range?

check.q: A line plot has 1 X above 1 1/2, 2 above 1 3/4, 2 above 2, 3 above 2 1/4 and 1 above 2 1/2. How many measurements?
check.why: Add the X marks: 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 + 1 = 9. There are 5 different values, but 9 measurements.

check.q: On that plot, which weight is the most common?
check.why: The tallest stack, 3 X marks, is above 2 1/4.

check.q: Crayons on a line plot go from 3 1/4 inches to 3 3/4 inches. What is the range?

lessons.title: Build Your Own Line Plot
lessons.mainIdea: To make a line plot, measure, choose a number line that fits the data, and place one X for each measurement.
reading: The class measured 8 pencils to the nearest half inch. The lengths were 5, 4 1/2, 6, 5, 5 1/2, 4 1/2, 5 and 6. To make a line plot, first find the smallest and largest. Those are 4 1/2 and 6. Draw a number line from 4 1/2 to 6. Mark every half inch: 4 1/2, 5, 5 1/2, 6.

Next, place the X marks. Go through the list one pencil at a time. 5 gets an X. 4 1/2 gets an X. 6 gets an X. The next 5 stacks a second X above 5. Keep going until every pencil has one X. Count your X marks at the end: 3 above 5, 2 above 4 1/2, 2 above 6, and 1 above 5 1/2. That is 3 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 8, one for each pencil.

Give the plot a *title*, like Pencil Lengths in Inches. Add a *label* for the unit under the number line. A common mistake is to skip a mark when no pencil has that length. Keep every half inch mark, even an empty one. Otherwise the spacing will lie. Another mistake is placing two X marks side by side. They must be stacked.

words.d: the name at the top of a graph that tells what the data is about
words on a graph that tell what the numbers or pictures mean, like Inches
measuring so each answer ends in 0 or 1/2, like 5 or 5 1/2

look.title: From List to Plot
look.text: Seven students measured how far they could jump, to the nearest half foot: 3, 3 1/2, 4, 3 1/2, 3 1/2, 4 1/2, 4. The smallest is 3 and the largest is 4 1/2, so the number line runs 3, 3 1/2, 4, 4 1/2. The stacks are 1 X above 3, 3 above 3 1/2, 2 above 4, and 1 above 4 1/2.
look.prompt: Check the stacks by adding them. Do you get 7? Which jump length is the most common?

check.q: Pencil lengths are 5, 4 1/2, 6, 5, 5 1/2, 4 1/2, 5 and 6. How many X marks go above 5?
check.why: The number 5 appears three times in the list, so it gets 3 X marks.

check.q: Data goes from 4 1/2 to 6 in half inches. Which marks belong on the number line?
check.why: Every half inch from smallest to largest must be marked, even ones with no X.

check.q: What happens if you skip a mark that has no X marks?
choices: The spacing on the number line becomes wrong
check.why: The gaps between marks must be equal, or distances on the plot no longer match the numbers.

lessons.title: Solving Problems With Data
lessons.mainIdea: A graph or table gives the numbers; you still choose the operation and check that the answer makes sense.
reading: Data displays answer questions only after you do some math. Pepper's line plot shows 9 weights. Ms. Chen asked: on how many Mondays did Pepper weigh less than 2 pounds? Find the stacks left of 2: 1 X above 1 1/2 and 2 above 1 3/4. Add them: 1 + 2 = 3 Mondays.

Some questions need two steps. The bar graph of name votes shows Biscuit 15, Nugget 10, Oreo 8 and Waffles 4. How many students voted for a name other than Biscuit? First add the others: 10 + 8 + 4 = 22. Or find the total, 37, and subtract 15 to get 22. Both routes should agree. If they do not, one has a mistake.

Always check the *reasonableness* of an answer. Suppose a question about 9 Mondays gives an answer of 15 Mondays. Something went wrong. If the pencil plot has 8 pencils, no answer about them can be bigger than 8. A quick estimate before you compute helps you catch a slip.

words.d: a problem that needs two operations, like add first and then subtract
whether an answer makes sense for the situation; a check you do after computing

look.title: Two Routes to One Answer
look.text: The picture graph of March reading shows Maya 12 books, Leo 10 books and Dario 20 books. The class goal was 50 books. Route one: add 12 + 10 + 20 = 42, then 50 − 42 = 8 books short. Route two: subtract each from 50 in turn: 50 − 12 = 38, 38 − 10 = 28, 28 − 20 = 8. Both routes give 8.
look.prompt: If Leo reads 6 more books and Maya reads 3 more, does the class reach 50? Show both routes.

check.q: Votes were Biscuit 15, Nugget 10, Oreo 8, Waffles 4. How many votes were not for Biscuit?
Pepper's plot has 1 X above 1 1/2, 2 above 1 3/4, 2 above 2, 3 above 2 1/4 and 1 above 2 1/2. How many Mondays was she 2 pounds or more?
check.why: Count X marks at 2 and to the right: 2 + 3 + 1 = 6.

check.q: A plot shows 8 pencils. A student says 11 pencils are shorter than 5 inches. What should the student do?
choices: Check the work, since 11 is more than 8
Change the scale of the plot
check.why: No answer about 8 pencils can be greater than 8, so 11 is not reasonable.

review.q: How many inches are in 3 feet?
How many grams are in 3 kilograms?
How many quarts are in 2 gallons?
review.why: Each gallon is 4 quarts, so 2 × 4 = 8 quarts.

review.q: A show is 200 minutes long. How long is that in hours and minutes?
Recess starts at 1:50 and ends at 2:20. How long is recess?
review.why: Jump 10 minutes to 2:00, then 20 minutes to 2:20. That is 30 minutes.

review.q: A bar graph has a scale of 10. A bar reaches halfway between the second and third lines. What does it show?
review.why: The second line is 20 and the third is 30, so halfway is 25.

review.q: Each smiley on a picture graph stands for 6 students. A row shows 3 and a half smileys. How many students?
A line plot of ribbon lengths has X marks at 1/4, 1/2, 1/2, 3/4, 3/4, 3/4 and 1 foot. What is the most common length?
review.why: The stack above 3/4 has 3 X marks, more than any other.
